# Indonesia

The wealth gradients this library holds for Indonesia: first the values to give OG-Core, then the measurements behind them. New to the terms? See the [glossary](../glossary.md).

## What to use in OG-Core

| OG-Core input | Tilt | From |
|---|---|---|
| `fert_gradient` | **by age**, table below (fertility tilt −0.38 plus the [age offsets](../methods/fertility-by-age.md)) | DHS 2017 |
| `infmort_gradient` | **−0.73** | DHS 2017 |
| `mort_gradient` | **−0.79** (ages 15–60) | [general gradient](../methods/general-gradient.md) at GNI $5,010 per person (~2024) |
| `imm_pctiles` | not covered by this library | — |

Every value is a **tilt** ([what that is](../glossary.md#tilt)). Convert it before passing it to OG-Core: `tilt / (100 × (1 − p))`, with p OG-Core's own rate at that age ([how](../methods/ogcore-units.md)).

**Fertility tilt by mother's age** (for `fert_gradient`; ages under 15 take the 15–19 value, 50 and over the 45–49 value):

| 15–19 | 20–24 | 25–29 | 30–34 | 35–39 | 40–44 | 45–49 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| −1.16 | −0.48 | −0.18 | −0.06 | −0.29 | −0.78 | −1.37 |

## Where these numbers come from

### Household surveys (DHS)

Latest survey, from [`data/gradient_library_latest.csv`](../../data/gradient_library_latest.csv). Earlier surveys are in `gradient_library.csv`.

| Measure | Survey | Tilt | Poorest-to-richest ratio | Poorest fifth → richest fifth |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Births per woman (TFR) | 2017 | **−0.38** | 1.4 | 2.9 · 2.6 · 2.3 · 2.3 · 2.1 |
| Infant deaths per 1,000 births (IMR) | 2017 | **−0.73** | 1.8 | 40 · 26 · 23 · 24 · 20 |
| Under-5 deaths per 1,000 births (U5MR) | 2017 | **−0.80** | 1.9 | 52 · 33 · 29 · 31 · 24 |

## Notes

- No census household-deaths module is available, so there is no measured adult-mortality gradient; use the general gradient (worked value below). The DHS rows (IDHS 2017) cover fertility and child mortality directly.
- Indonesia is the canonical tempo case: its TFR-by-wealth gradient is nearly flat while adolescent childbearing differs ~8× between poorest and richest quintiles — the gradient lives in the age pattern, not the total.
